current_answer: Some Danish firms that first reported AI use in 2023 hired less than their prior trend predicted: the authors report a roughly 9% relative employment gap by September 2025, concentrated in firms with fewer than 100 employees. Those firms were still growing; the gap is not a count of layoffs or proof AI caused it. This is a different Danish study from yesterday’s chatbot-encouragement comparison, which found no extra early-career-share decline through 2024. The populations, AI measures, outcomes and end dates differ. U.S. junior-entry warnings remain live, but no study here predicts whether your own job will go.

catalogue_card.question: Are AI-using firms already hiring less?
catalogue_card.text: A Danish firm-record study links first-time AI use to slower hiring, mainly at small firms. The gap is not a layoff count or proof that AI caused it.

summary: Danish firms first reporting AI use in 2023 had a roughly 9% trend-relative employment gap by September 2025 in the authors’ latest account; their central-bank abstract reports 11% slower growth.
The gap was concentrated at firms below 100 employees and appeared through fewer hires, not layoffs; the firms still grew.
This observational firm study does not overturn a separate Danish chatbot-encouragement null through 2024 or predict an individual job.
uncertainty: The new Danish firm study is observational: adopters and non-adopters may differ in unmeasured ways despite pre-trend and industry comparisons.
The central-bank abstract reports 11% slower employment growth; the authors’ CEPR exposition reports a roughly 9% trend-relative gap. The full specification difference was not verified.
The Danish study covers surveyed private non-financial firms with at least 10 employees and ends September 2025; the small-adopter group employs less than 2% of Danish workers.
Yesterday’s Danish null is a different sample, adoption proxy, outcome and time window, not a replication of this study.
